patches.reason: The cue in the scenario is a smell in the hallway — an external feature of the environment — which makes this context-dependent memory. This lesson defines state-dependent memory as a match in the learner's *internal* physiological or emotional state, and the MCAT tests that separation directly, so labelling an external cue as state-dependent teaches the distinction backwards.

patches.old: This also relates to state-dependent memory when internal or external states match.
patches.new: Keep the two forms apart: an external match — the same room, the same smell, the same background noise — is context-dependent memory, while an internal match — the same mood, the same level of caffeine or arousal — is state-dependent memory. Both follow from encoding specificity, and this scenario is the external case.
patches.reason: The published sentence folds external cues into state-dependent memory, contradicting the lesson's own definitions of the two terms; corrected alongside the repaired choice.

visual.title: The pipeline, the branches, and the two interferences
visual.alt: The flow from sensory memory, which holds almost everything for under a second, through working memory at about seven chunks for fifteen to thirty seconds, into long-term memory with no known limit, with attention gating the first transfer, encoding the second and retrieval running back; long-term memory branching into explicit, with episodic and semantic and the hippocampus, and implicit, with procedural, priming and conditioning and the basal ganglia and cerebellum; Baddeley's central executive over the phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad and episodic buffer; bars showing memory strength rising from structural through phonemic to semantic processing; and the two directions of interference.
visual.caption: Most memory questions come down to naming the step that failed. Material that was never attended to was never encoded, and no amount of retrieval cueing will bring it back.
